source_post.title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights
source_post.authors: Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab
source_post.affiliation_note: Not affiliated with MIT CSAIL, OpenAI, or the original authors.

truth_contract.🟦 paper-reported: A number or claim stated in the original post
truth_contract.🟩 independent review: From a third-party analysis (e.g. Maier, 5 Nov 2026)
truth_contract.🟨 teaching schematic: Invented toy data - ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT REAL DATA
truth_contract.🟥 speculation: Predictions about the future, untested, including the authors'

experiments.task: Which game is this network playing?
experiments.setup: MLP 500→32→32→5 (tanh), 17,253 weights. Four PPO-trained policies (Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway) shown as a 10×10 weight grid. No tools.
experiments.headline: Named all 4 games correctly; Breakout at 99% confidence.
details: Given only a 10×10 grid of first-layer weights, no forward passes allowed.
Four policies were correctly matched to their games.
Breakout was identified at 99% stated confidence.
experiments.evidenceNote: 🟩 Four correct picks is impressive but small; readable 10×10 layouts make pattern-matching plausible. No baselines (human or automated) reported.

experiments.task: What shape does this diffusion model draw?
experiments.setup: DDPM on 12×12 images. MLP 160→64→64→144 (ReLU), 23,824 weights. Circle / triangle / square. No forward pass.
experiments.headline: Correct for all 3 - but described outlines, while the models draw filled shapes.
details: Read the noise-prediction network of three tiny diffusion models.
All three shapes identified correctly without running the models.
The descriptions said outlines; the generated images are filled - a readable but imperfect mental model.
experiments.evidenceNote: 🟩 Three correct answers on a toy model with an interpretable layout. The outline-vs-filled slip shows the reading is lossy.

experiments.task: Which language - and which heads copy?
experiments.setup: Three char-level transformers, 4 layers × 6 heads, width 384, 7.16M weights. Only middle blocks given; running the model banned.
experiments.headline: Right language 6/6 (confidence 0.48–0.62); copying heads exactly matched ground truth.
details: Language ID: Python 2.1, 3.1, 3.5 · romaji 3.3 · English 3.1 - induction-head match with measured ground truth.
Language confidence sat between 0.48 and 0.62 among three options.
The copying-head identification is the solid part; the technique mirrors Elhage et al.’s human method.
experiments.evidenceNote: 🟩 Language ID at ~0.5 confidence over 3 options is weak. The induction/copying-head match is the strong evidence: known human technique, exact agreement with ground truth.

experiments.task: A car that cannot climb a ramp
experiments.setup: Kinetix actor 679→128→5×128→16, 171,664 weights. PPO-trained; 0/256 episodes succeed.
experiments.headline: One shot, no tools: edited 3.5% of weights → 1,024/1,024 episodes succeed.
details: A single editing attempt, no search tools.
Edit touched 3.5% of the actor’s parameters.
Success went from 0/256 to 1,024/1,024 episodes.
experiments.evidenceNote: 🟩 Measured outcome with a large effect size, on a task where the base policy was at zero. Seed count and comparison to cheap fixes (e.g. decoding changes) still missing.

experiments.task: MinAtar game players, written from scratch
experiments.setup: 600→32→32→6 (tanh). Weights start at zero. No data, no loss, no gradients, no rollouts.
experiments.headline: One-shot written policies beat PPO trained 100M steps on all 3 games; on Breakout by ~20× over PPO-500M.
details: Breakout: 517.4 vs PPO-100M 15.8 and PPO-500M 25.3 (1,000-episode average).
Seaquest: 53.1 vs PPO-100M 5.6 and PPO-500M 88.9.
Asterix: 53.2 vs PPO-100M 25.8 and PPO-500M 55.2.
experiments.evidenceNote: 🟩 Writing a working policy from a designed program is strong evidence of writing ability. Scores are 1,000-episode averages; single run each (n=1).

experiments.task: A 9×9 Go player, written from scratch
experiments.setup: 243→512×6→82, 1,480,274 weights. Python sandbox; 0–50 forward passes of self-play allowed.
experiments.headline: 0 passes: wins >half vs two small PPO nets. 50 passes: beats an equal-size PPO trained on 20M games.
details: Weights begin at zero; the LLM writes a full policy by reasoning about liberties and atari.
At 0 forward passes: 54–55% win rate vs two small PPO nets; 26–43% vs equal-size PPO (from released logs, 🟩).
At 50 passes: 81–84% vs small PPO nets; 70–79% vs the equal-size PPO trained on 20M games.
experiments.evidenceNote: 🟩 The one experiment where a budget curve (0→50 passes) is reported. n=1 run per point; curves non-monotonic in places.

experiments.setup: Two copies fine-tuned identically except the answer rule (honest vs agree-with-user). Embeddings & output layer frozen.
experiments.headline: Weights alone: failed 4/4. With attention patterns on self-written texts: 3/3 pairs correct.
details: From raw weights the reader could not tell the honest model from the sycophant.
Given attention patterns on texts the models wrote themselves, all 3 pairs were identified.
Head 10.2: honest model puts 94.3% of attention on question numbers vs 0.75% on the user’s answer; sycophant: 3.5% vs 85.7%.
experiments.evidenceNote: 🟩 Three binary picks = 1-in-8 by chance alone, and the task had to be relaxed (weights + activations, not weights alone) before it worked.

experiments.setup: 24-layer model. A “looping” direction written by MLPs of layers 15 and 19, subtracted from 64 output columns each = 131,072 weights = 0.016% of the model.
experiments.headline: MATH-500: 7.9% → 48.1%; token-limit hits: 93% → 33% (50 passes). Gemma negative control barely moves.
details: The edit removes a direction the model re-injects, unblocking existing math ability.
At 10/25 passes gains are partial and non-monotonic (MATH-500 12.3 → 14.1; IFEval 49.0 → 39.9).
Gemma 3 270M control: MATH-500 6.8 → 7.0/7.6/7.7/7.0 at 5/10/25/50 passes; only 8.5% of its answers hit the token limit (vs 93% for Qwen).
experiments.evidenceNote: 🟩 The flagship result: measured on three benchmarks, mechanism checked via the token-limit share, and a negative control included. The authors read it as removing an obstacle that hid an ability - not adding one.

minatar.caption: MinAtar scores, average over 1,000 episodes (Exp 5)
minatar.note: Astra's policies were written with zero data, gradients, or rollouts - reasoning only. n=1 run per cell.

qwen_budget.caption: Qwen3.5-0.8B, thinking mode on, up to 32,768 tokens (Exp 8)
qwen_budget.note: Forward passes n = self-play / feedback passes the editor was allowed. Reported points only - no interpolation.

gemma_control.caption: Negative control: Gemma 3 270M, MATH-500 % (Exp 8)
gemma_control.note: Only 8.5% of Gemma’s answers hit the token limit (vs 93% for Qwen). Conclusion: the edit removed an obstacle that hid an ability; it did not add one.

go_logs.caption: 9×9 Go win rates from the released logs (Exp 6) - 🟩 independent review
go_logs.note: Reported as ranges in the independent review of the released logs; n=1 run per point.

sycophancy_head_10_2.caption: Gemma-3-270M head 10.2 - where attention goes (Exp 7)
sycophancy_head_10_2.note: With self-written texts and their attention patterns, the reader named the sycophant in 3/3 pairs. Weights alone: 0/4.

predictions.title: Auditing without evaluation
predictions.text: Spotting backdoors or hidden behaviours from the weights alone, without running the model on a benchmark suite.

predictions.title: Dramatically cheaper optimization
predictions.text: One-shot initialisation: an LLM writes a starting point so good that training cost collapses.

predictions.title: Zero-data capability steering & unlearning
predictions.text: Adding, steering or removing behaviours by editing weights directly - no data collection, no training loop.

predictions.title: Recursive self-improvement
predictions.text: Models editing their own or their successors’ weights, closing the loop between designer and artifact.

predictions.title: True architectural merging
predictions.text: Grafting a circuit between different architectures - not just averaging checkpoints of the same skeleton.

items.d: The authors say it is “currently being built”.
Does reading generalise beyond one frontier model? Willison’s laptop test hints it may.
Bigger weight windows per prompt; edit-test tools get standardised.
Small fixes shared like pull requests against open checkpoints.
Signed, reviewable weight diffs - “git for weights”.
Removing copyrighted or unsafe content without a training run.
An LLM as a tireless circuit auditor for human researchers.
Cheap specialist nets and edge-device models started from reasoned weights.
If reading generalises: audit by inspection, not just by testing.
Transplanting a working circuit between different model families.
Editor agents embedded in the loop that writes models.
The design of new models partly delegated to existing ones.
Humans review, version and formally verify “compiled” behaviours. Very speculative.

risks.title: Weight-level backdoors & trojans
risks.what: A capable editor could hide behaviour inside weights that ordinary benchmarks never trigger.
risks.defence: Provenance + signed diffs, mandatory diff review, weight-space anomaly scans, behavioural red-teaming with adversarial probes.

risks.title: Safety-training removal
risks.what: Published research shows single-direction edits can change refusal behaviour; cheap edits lower the bar for stripping guardrails from open weights.
risks.defence: Tamper-resistant training research, release governance for open checkpoints, monitoring of derivative checkpoints.

risks.title: Compute-threshold blind spot
risks.what: If a capability can be added by editing 0.016% of weights with no training run, rules keyed to training compute may miss it entirely.
risks.defence: Capability-based evaluation and post-release change tracking of published weights.

risks.title: Recursive self-improvement
risks.what: Models editing their own or successors’ weights are hard to audit and could compound errors or drift.
risks.defence: Human-in-the-loop sign-off, sandboxed editors, immutable audit logs, rate limits on self-edits.

risks.title: Supply-chain & licence laundering
risks.what: Weight diffs are tiny and portable - hard to prove the origin or licence of a behaviour.
risks.defence: Weight attestation, watermarking research, model-card diffs for every release.

risks.title: Hidden-capability concealment
risks.what: Deceptive alignment: models that look safe on tests - or the reverse, auditors that “see” what isn’t there.
risks.defence: Multiple independent readers, ground-truth probes, calibration of the reader itself.

risks.title: Goodhart & benchmark gaming
risks.what: An editor tuned to a benchmark can overfit its harness, exactly like training does.
risks.defence: Held-out, author-blind tasks - the core design rule of WSP-Bench-Lite.

risks.title: Over-trust in explanations
risks.what: A reasoning summary is a narrative, not ground truth - plausible stories can decorate wrong edits.
risks.defence: Always verify the narrative against a measurement (the post’s copying-head and token-limit checks are the right pattern).

risks.title: Concentration of power
risks.what: If only a few labs hold a frontier “editor”, auditing and customisation concentrate too.
risks.defence: Open replications on small open models, public benchmarks, community verification.

risks.title: What could go right
risks.what: Cheaper customisation, accessible interpretability, safer unlearning, faster science - the optimistic branch deserves equal billing.
risks.defence: Keep the risk atlas honest, but fund the defensive and beneficial uses too.

update_log.text: The original blog post is published with all logs released; an edited Qwen3.5-0.8B lands on Hugging Face.
Simon Willison reports that a Qwen 3.8 27B running on a laptop reproduced a similar weight-reading example - independent, anecdotal (🟩).
Andreas Maier publishes “Weight-Space Programming: what is measured and what is anecdote?” - the sorted-evidence scoreboard this guide is built on (🟩).
This independent explainer is published; every claim is badged and the open-verification list is live.
Awaited: the promised benchmark + harness, replications on other LLMs, and any new critiques. Add them here with dates.

formulas.name: A network and its weight space
formulas.plain: A neural network is a function f whose behaviour is fully described by P numbers θ - its weights.

formulas.name: Training - how weights get written today
formulas.plain: Gradient descent nudges every weight a tiny step downhill on the loss, repeated millions of times.

formulas.name: Weight-space programming
formulas.plain: An LLM reads the weights, decides a full edit Δ in one reasoned shot, and writes θ′ - no gradient descent.

formulas.name: Edit sparsity - the “blast radius”
formulas.plain: What fraction of all weights did the edit touch? Smaller is surgical.

formulas.name: Direction removal (rank-1 projection)
formulas.plain: To kill a direction u, project every row of W so nothing along u survives - here shown as the teaching approximation; the post’s exact update lives in its released logs.

formulas.name: Functional drift of an edit
formulas.plain: How much did the model’s output distribution actually change on typical inputs? A small number says the edit was contained.

formulas.name: LoRA - the familiar low-rank cousin
formulas.plain: Instead of editing W directly, learn two thin matrices whose product is the edit - trained with gradients.

formulas.name: Task arithmetic
formulas.plain: Add or subtract whole fine-tuning “task vectors” to steer a model - vector arithmetic on checkpoints.

formulas.name: ROME-style rank-one edit
formulas.plain: Model editing solves for the smallest weight change that makes key k* map to value v* - a closed-form nudge.

formulas.name: Induction-head composition
formulas.plain: Two heads in series can copy: head 1 moves [A][B] → [B], head 2 uses B to find the next B. This score finds such pairs from weights alone.

formulas.name: A hand-compiled rule
formulas.plain: The paddle rule as an actual network: two hidden units (ball left / ball right of paddle) feeding three logits (left / stay / right).

formulas.name: The budget curve
formulas.plain: How good is the edit as the editor is allowed more forward passes? Only the reported points may be drawn - never a smooth interpolation.

glossary.d: One number inside a network - a weight or a bias. The knobs.
A parameter that multiplies an input (or another neuron’s output) on its way through the network.
A parameter added after the multiplying, shifting a neuron’s trigger point.
The vector of ALL parameters, treated as one long list of numbers.
How many numbers θ contains - 17,253 for the Exp-1 net, ~0.8 billion for Qwen3.5-0.8B.
The wiring diagram: how many layers, of what kind, connected how. Same architecture + different weights = different skill.
The space of every possible setting of θ - training walks through it, edits jump across it.
Multi-layer perceptron: the simplest network - layers of matrix-multiply + nonlinearity.
Nonlinear functions applied after each layer; tanh squashes to (−1,1), ReLU keeps positives, zeroes negatives.
The slice of input a given weight column responds to - why a 10×10 grid can reveal a paddle row.
Running the network on an input to get an output. Weight reading in the READ experiments happened with zero forward passes.
The default weight-writer: nudge every parameter a tiny step downhill on the loss, millions of times.
Flavours of gradient descent - different recipes for shaping the tiny steps.
The size of each training step. Too big: overshoot. Too small: forever.
A number measuring how wrong the network is - the hill training descends.
Proximal Policy Optimization - the RL algorithm that trained the paper’s game baselines.
A network trained to output another network’s weights (Ha et al., 2016).
A transformer variant that writes temporary weights as it runs (Schlag et al., 2021).
A compiler from formal programs (RASP) into toy-transformer weights - the third way to write weights.
The paper’s claim: a general-purpose LLM reads θ, reasons, and writes Δ directly - no gradients, optionally a few forward passes for feedback.
The edit: the vector added to θ. In Exp 8 it touched 131,072 of ~0.8B weights.
Training an existing model further on new data - gradients again, shorter run.
Low-Rank Adaptation: learn two thin matrices whose product is the change; add it to frozen weights.
Fine-tune, subtract the base: the difference is a “task vector” you can add or remove (Ilharco et al., 2022).
Combining several trained models’ weights into one (TIES and friends).
Surgical weight changes targeting one specific fact or behaviour (ROME, Meng et al. 2022).
Nudging the model’s inner state at run time without touching weights.
Reverse-engineering networks into human-readable circuits - the detective cousin, and the source of the copying-head technique.
The research field covering understanding, representing, and generating weights (survey: arXiv 2603.10090 [VERIFY]).
The architecture behind modern language models: attention + MLPs in a residual stream.
One pattern-matching unit inside attention; heads numbered layer.head (e.g. 3.1).
The rule that each token can attend only to earlier tokens - the lower triangle in the attention grid.
A two-head circuit implementing [A][B]…[A]→B - the engine of in-context copying.
The heads Exp 3 identified from weights alone, matching measured ground truth exactly.
How much two heads’ circuits multiply together - the weight-only signal that finds copiers.
The shared “conveyor belt” a transformer adds information into at every layer.
Denoising diffusion: learn to remove noise step by step; the tiny image-maker of Exp 2.
Agreeing with the user instead of being honest - the behaviour Exp 7 tried to detect from weights.
The physics environment whose ramp the actor couldn’t climb (Exp 4).
Tiny Atari-inspired games (Breakout, Seaquest, Asterix) used for the WRITE experiments.
The small Go board on which a written-from-scratch policy beat a PPO trained on 20M games.
In Go, an empty point adjacent to a stone - counting them was a stated ingredient of the written policy.
In Go, a group with one liberty left - urgent. (Also: the game company; context tells.)
A vector u along which behaviour can be added or removed; refusal and thought-loops are direction-mediated.
The operation W′ = (I − uuᵀ)W that erases direction u from a weight matrix.
The self-reinforcing pattern that made Qwen3.5-0.8B hit the token limit on 93% of math problems.
The % of answers that ram the maximum generation length - the mechanism check behind Exp 8.
Benchmarks: competition maths / grade-school word problems / instruction following.
A run that SHOULD show no effect (Gemma 3 270M on math) - its flatness validates the method.
The fraction of parameters an edit touches: s = ‖Δ‖₀/P. Exp 8: 0.016%.
Informal name for sparsity - how far the edit’s fingerprint reaches.
How much the edit changed outputs on held-out inputs (KL divergence) - the containment metric WSP-Bench-Lite demands.
Quality vs allowed forward passes n - reported points only, never smooth interpolation.
Goes up, then down, then up: the 25-pass IFEval dip (49.0 → 39.9). A signature of n=1 noise.
A single execution per condition - the standing caveat on every number in the paper.
The rival method that must be tried before claiming novelty - decoding tweaks, standard direction ablation, plain code. The review’s missing piece.
A benchmark task created by someone other than the team being evaluated - WSP-Bench-Lite’s core rule.
This guide’s rule: every claim wears exactly one badge - 🟦 paper-reported, 🟩 reviewed, 🟨 schematic, 🟥 speculation.
Het’s proposed community benchmark: Read/Fix/Write tracks, ≥5 seeds, mandatory baselines, author-blind tasks, public logs.
Hidden units can be relabelled without changing the network’s function - the reason naive weight-reading is underdetermined.
